content: Research focused on early removal of urinary catheters has shown an 85% significant reduction in catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) and improved hand hygiene compliance (58% vs. 5%). However, no studies were identified that specifically addressed patient values and preferences regarding this intervention. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) is confident that healthcare providers, policymakers, and patients would support this intervention, as it aligns with evidence-based practices and prioritizes infection prevention. The GDG also emphasized that implementing and adapting technical guidelines locally will require resources, including human resources for development and adaptation, as well as materials and equipment for execution. While some solutions may be low-cost, the feasibility of implementation depends on the presence of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs, IPC expertise, and the availability of necessary materials and equipment. The GDG is confident that this recommendation can be implemented in all countries, though feasibility may vary based on local infrastructure and resources. The GDG strongly recommends the development and implementation of evidence-based practice guidelines to reduce healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). These guidelines should be part of a broader multimodal improvement strategy, including healthcare worker education and training. The GDG also identified research gaps, particularly in evaluating the effectiveness of local adaptation and implementation of IPC guidelines, and suggested conducting situational analyses to assess existing guidelines and their mechanisms for achieving cultural change. The GDG highlighted the importance of embedding IPC education and training into healthcare facilities. This training should involve teamand task-based strategies, including bedside and simulation training, to reduce HAIs and combat AMR. Evidence from 15 studies shows that practical, hands-on IPC education involving frontline healthcare workers is associated with decreased HAIs and improved hand hygiene compliance. However, due to varied methodologies and outcomes, no meta-analysis was performed. The GDG unanimously agreed that IPC education and training should be implemented for all healthcare workers using participatory approaches. The GDG emphasized that IPC education should be part of a comprehensive health facility education strategy, including orientation for new employees and continuous education for existing staff, regardless of their role. Special circumstances, such as outbreaks, may require ad hoc training. The GDG also supported embedding IPC training within clinical practice rather than delivering it as a standalone activity. Three categories of healthcare workers were identified as targets for IPC training: IPC specialists, all healthcare workers involved in patient care, and other personnel supporting healthcare delivery, such as cleaners and administrative staff. The GDG strongly recommended incorporating in-service mentorship into health facilities, as it has been shown to achieve behavior change in other fields. For example, IPC link practitioners could serve as unit-based resources or champions. At the national level, the GDG recommended that IPC programs support education and training as a core function. This includes developing national IPC curricula in collaboration with academic institutions for both pre-graduate and postgraduate courses. Pre-graduate curricula should provide basic IPC education, while postgraduate curricula should train professionals to become IPC specialists. National IPC programs should also provide guidance for in-service training at the facility level, covering core IPC competencies for all professional categories. The GDG emphasized the importance of facility-based HAI surveillance to guide IPC interventions and detect outbreaks, including AMR surveillance. Timely feedback of results to healthcare workers and stakeholders is critical. Evidence from 13 studies shows that hospital-based surveillance systems are associated with reduced HAIs, including bloodstream infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, surgical site infections, and CAUTIs. Active surveillance methods, such as prospective surveillance, are recommended over passive methods due to their higher sensitivity. The GDG noted that HAI surveillance should be based on national recommendations and standard definitions, customized to the facility's resources and objectives. Surveillance should provide data on infection incidence, AMR patterns, high-risk populations, and the impact of interventions. The responsibility for planning and conducting surveillance typically lies with the IPC committee and team, requiring expertise in statistics and epidemiology. Staff conducting surveillance should receive education on microbiology and communicable diseases. The GDG also highlighted the critical role of quality microbiology and laboratory capacity in enabling reliable HAI surveillance. Hospital-based surveillance systems should be linked to integrated public health infection surveillance systems, with immediate reporting of diseases of concern to public health authorities.
